title: Transactional database
purpose: Measure transactional throughput and latency against a PostgreSQL instance this agent creates in a container and destroys when the module ends - never against a database already on this machine.

implementation.note: The server and the load tool both come from the pinned image. pgbench is run through container::Sandbox::exec with a fixed argument vector, so no database driver exists in this workspace and nothing on the host is involved. See docs/adr/0006-module-isolation.md.

dependencies: A container runtime (Docker or Podman) whose daemon is reachable
1 GiB of free memory for the sandboxed database, including its dataset, which is held in a tmpfs rather than on disk

safety.target: a PostgreSQL container this module starts, published on 127.0.0.1 on a port the runtime assigns
never: a database already running on this machine
an operator-supplied host, port, socket or credential
an image that is not pinned to a digest
safety.note: docs/THREAT-MODEL.md (T-DB) is binding and permanent. This module has no configuration for a host and no code path that could reach one: it gets a sandboxed server or it reports itself not measured. A database module that quietly measured the operator's production database - and, being read-write, wrote to it - would be the worst thing this program could do. The absence of that path is the mitigation.

sandbox.user: 999:999, the image's own postgres account. The container is never root: the entrypoint's chown-and-drop dance is skipped rather than enabled with capabilities, so CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE, FOWNER, SETUID and SETGID are never held.
sandbox.capabilities: all dropped, no-new-privileges set, no host path mounted, no device passed
sandbox.data_directory: /var/lib/postgresql/data on a 512 MiB tmpfs owned by the service account, mode 0700
sandbox.memory: 1 GiB, covering the tmpfs and the service together - they are one budget, because tmpfs pages are charged to the container's cgroup
sandbox.readiness: pg_isready -q -h 127.0.0.1, run inside the container. A TCP connect from the host is not a readiness signal: Docker's userland proxy answers it as soon as the container exists.
sandbox.lifetime: removed when the module returns, on every path including failure. Anything a killed run leaves behind carries this agent's label and is reaped at the start of the next one.

preparation: pgbench -i -q -s 10 builds the dataset before anything is measured. A build that fails is a Precondition error naming the cause, not a run full of zeroes.
calibration: Phases are fixed-duration rather than calibrated to a work size: a repetition count that varied with the profile would make two runs of the same machine incomparable. Throughput phases run unlimited; latency phases run rate-limited below capacity.
warmup: None beyond the dataset build and its vacuum. pgbench's own connection establishment is excluded from the reported tps, which is the figure taken.

workloads.represents: A cached CMS, a read replica, an API reading a hot table

workloads.description: Mean select-only latency at an offered 200 tx/s across 4 clients, measured from when each transaction was due
workloads.represents: What a page waits on a read query at a load the machine sustains

workloads.description: The slow 5% of the same phase, ESTIMATED from the mean and standard deviation
workloads.represents: A floor on the read tail - useful for `is this acceptable`, wrong for `what is my worst case`

workloads.description: Mean read-write latency at an offered 200 tx/s across 4 clients
workloads.represents: Commit path latency, which is where durability shows up

workloads.description: The tail on the commit path, ESTIMATED the same way
workloads.represents: A floor on the write tail

repetitions.note: Phase durations are fixed at 20 s regardless of profile, so this module has no per-profile repetition table. A profile-dependent phase length would make two runs of the same machine incomparable, which is the opposite of what a profile is for.

validation: A latency phase whose schedule lag exceeded the tolerance is reported GeneratorSaturated and degrades the result: transactions issued late do not describe the load the phase claims to have offered.
A phase that processed no transactions is withheld rather than reported as a throughput of zero, which would read as a very slow machine instead of a phase that did not run.

A phase that lost clients part-way through is withheld. pgbench still reports a rate for one, computed over the whole window it was asked for including the part after the clients were gone, so the figure looks ordinary and is not a measurement of anything.
An image that is not pinned to a digest is not run at all.
abort_conditions: no container runtime, or a runtime whose daemon does not answer
the container exits during startup, in which case its own log is reported
cleanup: The container is removed when the module ends, including on failure. Anything a crashed run leaves behind carries this agent's label and is removed at the start of the next run - which is the only cleanup available, because the release profile aborts on panic and nothing runs on SIGKILL.
limitations: pgbench shares the container with the server, so its CPU is CPU the server did not get. Every figure here is a floor, not an estimate.

The 95th percentile is ESTIMATED from the mean and standard deviation assuming a normal distribution. A latency distribution is not normal and its tail is exactly where that matters, so it is a floor on the real p95.
The data directory is a tmpfs. The WAL is written and fsynced, but to RAM, so these figures describe the server and the CPU rather than the disk. storage.mixed is where the disk is measured.

The workload is pgbench's built-in one, which its own documentation calls loosely based on TPC-B. This is not TPC-B, it is not a TPC result, and no figure here may be compared to a published TPC number.
MariaDB and MySQL are not measured. No open-model load tool ships in their official images, and a closed-loop one would report latencies of a server that was politely never overloaded.

Each metric is one phase and one figure, so no coefficient of variation is computed and stability_cv_bound is not enforced against these. On an oversubscribed host the throughput figures were observed to vary by more than a factor of two between runs; comparing single runs across machines of very different core counts should account for that.

scoring.note: The write path carries the most weight because it is the one that cannot be cached away and the one a commit waits on. Both estimated percentiles carry half the weight of the means they are derived from: they are a normal approximation, not an observed percentile, and a tail estimate should not move a category score as much as a measurement does. Reference anchors are declared targets, not measurements. See docs/SCORING-SYSTEM.md.
